findings.message: When deploymentId is given, voidDeployment uses it alone and ignores input.environment, which is still required. It only checks that the id belongs to the release. The environment the caller named is never checked against the record. void_deployment is a destructive MCP/chat tool, so a mismatched pair voids a record in a different environment without warning. That includes the releasing Prod record, which un-releases proposals. Fix: when deploymentId is given, also require the record's environment to match lower(input.environment), or refuse the call; then add a mismatch case to the void-by-id test.
findings.scenario: MCP void_deployment {projectKey:'VID', version:'v1', environment:'Dev', deploymentId:<id of the live Prod record>, reason:'bad dev'} → the Prod deployment is voided and the release's proposals go back to verified, though the caller named Dev.

findings.message: The migration creates the unique index on (project_id, lower(name)) without first resolving existing case-duplicates. Before this round, upsertEnvironment matched names exactly, so it could create them. On any database that already has 'Prod' and 'prod' in one project, the migration fails and blocks the deploy. Fix: merge or rename the duplicates first, moving deployments to the kept row, then create the index. Add a migration test that seeds a duplicate.
findings.scenario: A project where someone ran upsertEnvironment {name:'prod'} before this fix has both 'Prod' and 'prod' → running migration 0008 fails with 'could not create unique index environment_name_ci' and the release cannot migrate.

findings.message: nextStep returns 'No Prod stage' whenever the furthest reached stage has nothing after it in order, even when the project has a Prod stage that was never deployed. upsertEnvironment appends new environments after Prod (max(position)+1), and recordDeployment accepts any environment. So a release that reached a stage placed after Prod shows 'No Prod stage' and offers no way to deploy to Prod. Fix: return 'No Prod stage' only when no stage has isProd. Otherwise, when nothing follows the last reached stage, offer the first Prod stage that isn't deployed. Add this case to the table test.
findings.scenario: Stages Dev(1, deployed), QA(2), UAT(3), Prod(4, isProd, never deployed), DR(5, deployed) → nextStep gives {label:'No Prod stage', environment:null}. The page shows 'No Prod stage' with no Deploy button, though Prod exists and was never reached.

findings.message: assignProposals counts live Prod deployments once, at the start, with no lock on the release. recordDeployment (Prod) can commit between that count and the release_id updates. It releases only the proposals it saw, and the newly assigned one stays in a live release that it never shipped with. That is the same 'live release with an unreleased proposal' outcome this fix is meant to prevent. Fix: lock the release row (select … for update) in both assignProposals and recordDeployment before checking or releasing. Add a two-session race test.
findings.scenario: Session A runs setReleaseProposals(v1, [a, b]) and counts live = 0. Session B runs recordDeployment(v1, Prod, deployed), sees only a, releases a and commits. A then sets b.release_id = v1 and commits → v1 is live but b stays 'verified'.

findings.message: removeEnvironment now resolves the row case-insensitively and puts env.name in its error message. But it still returns `removed: input.name`, which is the caller's spelling, not the stored name. This is the same mismatch that was fixed for the ReleaseDeployed event. Return env.name.

The duplicate check depends only on the new case-insensitive index. If a rename collides with another environment in a different case, the caller gets a raw unique-violation error instead of a clear refusal. Fix: before the update, look up the new name with envByName and refuse when it belongs to another environment.
findings.scenario: upsertEnvironment {name:'QA', rename:'prod'} on a project that has 'Prod' → raw 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint environment_name_ci' error.

findings.message: The new test feeds matchRoute already-decoded strings. It never checks the premise the fix rests on: that Next 16 passes catch-all params to page.tsx already decoded. If that premise is wrong, '%20' and '%2F' stay encoded and nothing fails. Add a test through the page/params path, or cite the Next behaviour.
